rationale: B wins because it does the editor's job on proof, not just packaging: it turns the margin claim into a testable bridge with sample size, denominators, capex, confounders, and selective-disclosure risk. A's "An unprofitable public salad chain is betting its margin story on machines" is the right story, but it stops one question early; B's "whether unit-level gains actually reach the bottom line, or get eaten by capex, G&A, and retrofit cost" is the sharper version a business reporter can use. A is good material, just a little too content to frame. B interrogates.
gaps_in_A: "category-creation" over-inflates the first angle; Sweetgreen shifting store format is a deployment and operations story, not proof a new category exists.
"automation live mostly in pilots and demo units" is useful context, but it is not in the supplied facts; bring a source or cut it.

"One retrofitted Sweetgreen, before and after the conveyor" is smart but not live; the set admits, "This angle does not exist until that data does," so it belongs in prepare/hold, not beside announcement-ready angles.

"restaurant-level versus company-level margin definitions" is necessary, but the profitability angle misses capex, retrofit cost, and cash burn; without the cost side, the net-profitability bridge is half-built.
gaps_in_B: "The prevailing belief is that a company that hasn't reached profitability should be conserving capital" invents a counterparty; bring an analyst, investor note, filing risk, or kill the contrarian label.
"robot line runs at a better margin than its people line" is sharper than it is fair; the update says automated versus traditional stores, not a clean robots-versus-people margin comparison.
"That's the decision other operators are weighing right now" turns one company's rollout into an industry trend without evidence.
"it's the one with real numbers behind it" oversells the retrofit angle; the supplied margin figures are only a range, and no retrofit cost or payback numbers exist yet.
